name: The Caldwell household
head: caldwell_billy

arrival.note: 'At what time Caldwell took up his residence near Fort Dearborn is not definitely known, but probably about the year 1820.' The word 'probably' is the source's and the grade carries it. A SECOND COMPILATION PRINTS THE YEAR FLAT, AND THE GRADE STILL DOES NOT MOVE. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago vol. 1 (1895), printed pages 78-79, the table headed LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830 (data/research/books/records/moses_kirkland_v1_actual_settlers_pre_1830.json). It is an 1895 compilation crediting Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pp. 37-8 three lines above itself, every row transcription_mediated and none scan_verified, so NOTHING READ OFF IT IS GRADED ABOVE `inferred` HERE. Row bk_mose1_as_006 reads 'Caldwell, Billy', nativity Michigan, YEAR 1820, remarks 'Paid taxes in 1825, voted in 1826'. Where Andreas hedges with 'probably', the table prints 1820 in a year column with no hedge in it. THAT IS NOT ENOUGH TO PROMOTE THIS FIELD and it is deliberately not promoted: an 1895 compilation working from Hurlbut is not an independent witness to a date of 1820, and a hedge answered by a table is still a hedge. What it is worth is recorded and no more. WHAT DOES NOT FOLLOW: the table's own preamble bounds it BEFORE 1830 and its remarks are civic acts of 1825-1830. A man on it is not thereby at Chicago on 1835-07-01, and this edit moves no residence, no `present_on_scene_date` and no grade. The identity is the books crosswalk's landed merge (T-0961) and is not re-opened here.

reason_for_coming.value: The country trade at the forks
reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THIS HOUSEHOLD'S OWN RECORDED TRADE, WHICH IS NOT ITS MOTIVE. The head is recorded as interpreter, and this names the documented draw that trade answered in this town in this decade. It does not claim to know why these people came. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

basis.note: arrival_fill.trade_reasons.the_country_trade — the head's recorded trade is evidence about this household, and the draw it answered is the reason the record will carry until a source states one.

replaceable_by.match: a source that says why this household came, or a committed source that apportions the town's arrivals between the land sales, the canal and the harbour works

lives_at.note: TWO CANDIDATE LOCATIONS AND NO WAY TO CHOOSE, so the field is null. (1) Andreas: 'There was also a house built for him by the Department for Indian Affairs on the North Side near where is now the corner of State Street and Chicago Avenue' - and elsewhere calls it probably the first frame building in Chicago after Robert Kinzie's store, erected in 1828. That house is not in data/structures/ and is well north of the modelled blocks. (2) A list of the settlement's residents Andreas prints puts 'small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell, an Indian chief, who was also interpreter for the agency' in the vicinity of Cobweb Castle at the foot of State Street. Those are two different houses in two different places and neither is dated to 1835. Linking him to robinson_caldwell_cabins would be worse than either: that record's evidence is Wau-Bun's sentence about ROBINSON, and Caldwell's name reached its filename by a different route.

works_at.note: The agency's interpreter worked where the agency's business was done, and the government blacksmith shop this dataset holds stands beside the agency house. Inferred: no source puts this man in this building.

present_on_scene_date.note: PRESENT ON 1 JULY 1835 UNDER EITHER OF THE TWO DATINGS THIS PROJECT HOLDS, which is the one thing about his last Chicago years that is not in dispute. Andreas has him leading the assembly and the march to the Missouri in 1836; chicagology_lastwardance puts the last war dance at Chicago on 18 August 1835. Both are after the scene date. Derived rather than documented because it is an inference from two departure dates, not a statement that he was here in July.

persons.name: Billy Caldwell (Sauganash)

birth_year.note: 'Born about the year 1780' - the source's own approximation. Andreas elsewhere gives his death as 28 September 1841 'at the age of sixty-two', which would put the birth at 1778-79; the two figures do not agree and neither is adopted over the other.

age_on_scene_date.note: About 55 on 1 July 1835, on a birth year the source itself qualifies with 'about' and which its own death notice contradicts by a year or two.

occupation.note: Interpreter to the United States Indian agency at Chicago under Col. T. J. V. Owen: Andreas's account of the agency names the establishment - Gholson Kercheval and James Stuart as sub-agents, 'Billy Caldwell (Sauganash) as interpreter; David McKee as blacksmith, and Joseph Porthier as striker'. He had been appointed a justice of the peace for Peoria County in 1826 and appears on the poll lists of 1826 and 1830, usually officiating as one of the clerks of the election.

appearance_bounds.source_title: Fifth census of the United States, 1830 — the division headed 'Peoria & Putnam Counties & Territory attached'
appearance_bounds.identity_rule: Surname and given name both agree between the 1830 reading 'Billy Caldwell' and the town person 'Billy Caldwell (Sauganash)' in household hh_caldwell_billy. The 1830 line is carried as EARLIER EVIDENCE for that person and grades nothing on its own.
appearance_bounds.note: A BOUND ON PRESENCE IN A DISTRICT, AND NOT AT CHICAGO. The division is headed 'Peoria & Putnam Counties & Territory attached' and the schedule never writes the word Chicago — the Fox River and Du Page settlements are inside it — so this row bounds presence in that district in the summer of 1830 and puts no body in the town, which is why `here_by` is null. The record's own note says it first: 'Presence in that district in the summer of 1830; not a Chicago residence, and never an 1835 one'. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source EARLIER than the scene date corroborates and dates and never promotes, and a source LATER than it does not promote either. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT: the leaf is read scan_verified off the federal schedule, and what no source states is that the head of family on it is the person on this card. data/research/census_1830/resident_crosswalk.json joins them on a name agreement and says in terms that it grades nothing on its own. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

persons.note: THE MAN THE SAUGANASH HOTEL IS NAMED AFTER, which is how this dataset first met him: 'It was suggested to Mark that he should name his house after some great man. He could think of no greater personage than Billy Caldwell and so his tavern became celebrated as the "Sauganash."' Andreas: son of a Colonel Caldwell, an Irish officer in the British army at Detroit, and a Potawatomi mother; born about 1780; educated at the Jesuit schools of Detroit and fluent in French and English besides several Indian languages; secretary to Tecumseh from about 1807 until Tecumseh's death and present at the Thames on 5 October 1813; a captain in the British Indian Department as late as 1816. By the treaty of Prairie du Chien of 1829 he was granted two and a half sections on the Chicago River, about six miles up the North Branch, and by the treaties of 1832 and 1833 annuities aggregating $1,000; he sold the land early. When John Watkins started his school in 1832 Caldwell offered to pay the tuition and buy books and clothes for any Indian children who would attend.

The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

research_note: THE INTERPRETER OF THE AGENCY, THE NAMESAKE OF THE TOWN'S BEST-KNOWN TAVERN, AND A MAN WHO LEFT WITH HIS PEOPLE. STANDING CONSTRAINT. AGENTS.md: the final removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago occurred in August 1835, inside this project's first target year and six weeks AFTER the scene date; Native presence, representation and depiction are not research gaps to be filled by inference, and v1 ships no human figures at all. This record is a dataset entry that states what named sources say about a named person and adds nothing. It carries review_required so that no scene containing it can be marked released before the consultation the project has committed to. ANDREAS AND THIS PROJECT'S OTHER SOURCE DISAGREE BY A YEAR ABOUT THE REMOVAL ITSELF and the disagreement is recorded here rather than resolved: Andreas, 'In 1836, under the leadership of Captain Russell the Government Agent, and Billy Caldwell, the Indians to the number of nearly twenty-five hundred assembled for the last time at Chicago, to receive their payments and then take up their line of march for their new home on the Missouri, at Council Bluffs'; chicagology_lastwardance, transcribing a 1910 Tribune account, dates the last great war dance to 18 August 1835. AGENTS.md takes the 1835 dating as the project's standing constraint. Under either, 1 July 1835 is before it, and this household is in the scene. He died at Council Bluffs on 28 September 1841. BOTH FLAGS WERE FALSE UNTIL 2026-08-16 AND THE PARAGRAPH ABOVE SAID OTHERWISE. The sentence 'It carries review_required so that no scene containing it can be marked released' has been in this record since it was written, and `review_required` was never once set: the claim blocked nothing and read to every later agent as though it did. Nothing else about the record moved, and nothing was researched to justify the change — `touches_removal` is set from this record's own committed text, which quotes Andreas putting this man at the head of the march to the Missouri. ROADMAP K34 found it by reading the prose against the field, and tools/measure_review_constraint.py asserts the two agree from here on.
